preamble: Deaspiration of [pʰ] to plain [p]. In Ancient Greek it results from Grassmann's law, a dissimilation whereby the first of two aspirates in successive syllables loses aspiration; it shows up in reduplicated perfects of φ-initial roots and in inherited words such as παχύς 'thick' (PIE *bʰénǵʰus, with *bʰ > pʰ and then deaspiration before the following χ). Unconditioned loss of aspiration is found in Sinhala, which, unlike most Indo-Aryan languages, lost the aspirated series entirely in its inherited vocabulary (Pali puppha > Eḷu pupa 'flower'); this loss is often attributed to a South Dravidian substrate. In the Nguni languages Xhosa and Zulu, [pʰ] loses its aspiration after a homorganic nasal, most visibly in class 9/10 nouns formed with the prefix iN- (Xhosa and Zulu phila 'to be well' > impilo 'health'); Wikipedia's prenasalisation tables label the rule "Aspiration is lost on obstruents". Zulu realizes the resulting plain stop as an ejective, while Xhosa ejectives are plain tenuis stops except in careful pronunciation or salient positions (Wikipedia, Xhosa language).

examples.to: πέφυκα péphūka 'I have grown, I am by nature'
examples.note: Grassmann's law: the reduplicating syllable loses aspiration before the aspirated root-initial φ.
Root-internal Grassmann's law: *bʰ became pʰ in Greek and then lost its aspiration before the aspirate χ of the next syllable; cognate Sanskrit bahú 'much'.
Unconditioned loss of aspiration (with degemination); Pali stands in for the Middle Indo-Aryan input. Aspirated letters survive in the Sinhala script only for Sanskrit and Pali loanwords.
